difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: one divisibility rule combined with a single permutation count, well under 1.5 minutes.
stem: How many 4-digit positive integers divisible by 3 can be formed using only the digits $\{1, 3, 4, 6, 7\}$, such that no digit appears more than once in a number?

solution.quick: A 4-digit number with distinct digits from $\{1,3,4,6,7\}$ uses all but one digit. The five digits sum to 21, so the digit sum is $21-d$ for the omitted digit $d$. This is divisible by 3 only when $d\in\{3,6\}$. Each of the 2 digit sets can be arranged in $4!=24$ ways, giving $2\times24=48$, option **(B)**.

steps.title: Divisibility rule
steps.body: An integer is divisible by 3 if and only if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. The order of the digits does not matter, only which digits are used.

steps.title: Which digit sets work?
steps.body:
Choosing 4 distinct digits from 5 means leaving out exactly one digit $d$. The sum of all five digits is

$$1+3+4+6+7 = 21,$$

so the chosen digits sum to $21-d$. Since $21$ is a multiple of 3, $21-d$ is a multiple of 3 exactly when $d$ is:

| Omitted $d$ | Digits used | Sum | Divisible by 3? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 3, 4, 6, 7 | 20 | No |
| 3 | 1, 4, 6, 7 | 18 | **Yes** |
| 4 | 1, 3, 6, 7 | 17 | No |
| 6 | 1, 3, 4, 7 | 15 | **Yes** |
| 7 | 1, 3, 4, 6 | 14 | No |

steps.title: Count arrangements
steps.body:
Each valid set has 4 distinct non-zero digits, so every ordering is a genuine 4-digit number (there is no leading-zero issue). The number of orderings is

$$4! = 24 \text{ per set}.$$

steps.title: Total
steps.body:
$$2 \text{ sets} \times 24 = 48.$$

For comparison, all ${}^5P_4 = 120$ distinct-digit numbers can be formed, and 48 of them are divisible by 3. The answer is **(B)**, matching the official key.

solution.teaching:
**Why the digit-sum rule works.** Every power of 10 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 3 ($10 = 9+1$, $100 = 99+1$, and so on). So a number $\overline{abcd} = 1000a+100b+10c+d$ leaves the same remainder as $a+b+c+d$. Divisibility by 3 therefore depends only on the **multiset of digits**, not on their order.

**Turning it into a counting problem.** Because order is irrelevant for divisibility, split the count into two independent stages:

1. *Choose* which digits to use, and keep only the choices whose sum is a multiple of 3.
2. *Arrange* each good choice. With $k$ distinct digits and no zero among them, there are $k!$ arrangements. If 0 were available you would subtract the arrangements that start with 0.

**The complement trick.** When you pick $k$ digits out of $n$, it is often quicker to look at the $n-k$ digits you leave out. Here you leave out just one digit. The total sum $21$ is already a multiple of 3, so the remaining sum is a multiple of 3 exactly when the omitted digit is. That turns five sum checks into one glance: omit 3 or omit 6.

**Applying it here.** 2 good digit sets × $4! = 24$ arrangements each gives **48** numbers.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: 24 counts the arrangements of only one valid digit set. Both $\{1,4,6,7\}$ (omit 3) and $\{1,3,4,7\}$ (omit 6) work.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: 2 valid digit sets × $4! = 24$ arrangements = 48, matching the official key.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: 72 = 3 × 24 would need three valid digit sets, but only two of the five possible omissions give a digit sum divisible by 3.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: 12 is half the arrangements of a single set and does not arise from any correct count. Each valid set alone already gives 24 numbers.

solution.shortcut: The total digit sum 21 is divisible by 3, so omit a digit that is itself divisible by 3 (3 or 6). That gives 2 sets × 4! = 48.
solution.commonTrap: Counting only one valid digit set (answer 24), or forgetting that the order of the digits does not affect divisibility by 3 and so trying to test individual numbers.

transcription.notes: Transcribed from the official paper rendering and independently checked against it. The digit set is typeset in the paper as {1, 3, 4, 6, 7} (the text layer shows irregular spacing '{1, 3,4, 6, 7}'); it is rendered here with uniform spacing. Options match in order.

answerVerification.method: Blind independent re-solve + Python check agrees with official key
answerVerification.checkCode:
from itertools import permutations
print(sum(1 for p in permutations([1,3,4,6,7],4) if int(''.join(map(str,p)))%3==0))  # 48
answerVerification.notes: Blind solve: the five digits sum to 21, so omitting d leaves a multiple of 3 only for d = 3 or 6; 2 sets x 4! = 48. Brute-force enumeration of all 120 distinct-digit arrangements also gives 48, which agrees with the official key (B).
